opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because it's really how physics gets done in practice. When I face a hard problem, say computing some subtle effect in the image of a black hole, I almost never attack the full thing head-on. I first ask: what's the simplest version of this problem that still has the essential difficulty in it? Maybe I turn off the spin, or work in flat space, or take some limit where the equations simplify. I solve that, I check that the answer makes sense, and then I build back up.

What I've noticed with the models is that they can be remarkably good at warm-ups when you hand them the warm-up. If you say "first do the non-rotating case," they'll often nail it. And when I gave one a problem I'd spent a long time on, it initially couldn't get it. But once I gave it a simpler related problem, it solved that, and then it went back and cracked the harder one. That was a striking moment for me. It suggested the capability was there, and what was missing was the scaffolding.

So what I'd love to see is the models doing that themselves. Not waiting for me to propose the toy problem, but recognizing, "This is hard, I'm not converging. Let me find a special case I can solve exactly, use it to build intuition, and use it as a check on the general answer." That's research taste. Choosing the right warm-up is a skill in itself. A good one isn't just easier. It isolates the key obstacle, and its answer constrains what the general answer can look like.

The other piece is using the warm-up as a consistency check. When I get a general result, I immediately ask whether it reduces to the known answer in the appropriate limit. Models could do much more of that kind of self-verification, deliberately constructing limits and special cases to test their own work. If they internalize that loop of simplifying, solving, generalizing and checking, I think they'll move from being very capable assistants to being real collaborators on frontier problems.

r001.rationale: It proposes working in flat space as one way to simplify the black-hole problem while retaining its essential difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says models should choose a suitable toy problem themselves instead of waiting for a person to propose one.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the way I actually do research, and I think the way most theoretical physicists do it, is almost never to attack the real problem head-on. The real problem is usually too hard. You don't know the right variables, you don't know which effects matter, you don't even know what the answer should look like. So what you do is you find a toy version of it, a warm-up problem, and you solve that first.

In my own work, a lot of what I care about is black holes and the structure of light that orbits very close to the horizon, the photon ring. The honest question is, what does a realistic, spinning black hole surrounded by turbulent plasma look like through an interferometer? That's a nightmare. So you start with Schwarzschild, no spin. Then you add spin. Then you do a thin ring of emitters instead of a full disk. Each of those stages isn't a detour, it's where you actually learn what's going on. You figure out which quantities are universal, which approximations are safe, which ones secretly break.

So when I think about what I'd want from AI models, there are a few things.

The first is just to do this at all, and to do it deliberately. Right now, when you give a model a hard problem, the tendency is to go straight at it and produce something that looks like a full answer. I'd much rather it said, this is hard, here's a simplified version I'm confident I can solve exactly, let me do that first and then tell you what I learned. The willingness to shrink the problem is a sign of maturity, not weakness.

The second is choosing the right warm-up. This is really the skill. A bad warm-up problem is one that's easy for the wrong reasons, where the simplification kills exactly the feature you care about. If I'm trying to understand how spin affects the photon ring and I set spin to zero, I've learned nothing about my actual question. A good warm-up keeps the essential difficulty and throws away everything else. I'd want models to be able to articulate why a given toy model is a faithful miniature of the real thing, what it preserves, what it discards, and what you therefore can and cannot conclude from it.

The third is the step back up. Solving the toy problem is only half of it. The other half is extracting the lesson and carrying it to the next level of realism. Which structure survived? Which parameter turned out to control everything? Models are often quite good at the first part and then they don't actually use what they found. They'll solve the simplified case and then treat the full problem as if from scratch. I'd want a kind of ladder, where each rung is informed by the one below it.

And then finally, there's a point about honesty. A warm-up problem is also a calibration tool. If the model can't get the toy case right, in a regime where I know the exact answer, then I know not to trust it on the hard case. So I'd actually want models to volunteer that, to say, here's a limit where this reduces to something known, let's check I reproduce it, before going anywhere interesting. That's how I check my own calculations, and it's how I'd check a collaborator's, human or otherwise.

So, to sum up, I'd like them to behave less like an oracle and more like a good graduate student. Not the one who tries to prove the whole theorem on day one, but the one who comes back and says, I couldn't do the full thing, but I did this special case, here's what it taught me, and here's what I think the next step is. That's what real progress looks like.

r001.rationale: The response proposes Schwarzschild and other simplified cases as warm-ups, but does not identify the flat-space limit.

r002.rationale: It says models should choose the right warm-up themselves and explain why the toy problem preserves the essential features of the research question.

astra-6.text:
I’d like them to get better at choosing the warm-up problem themselves. In research, when you’re stuck on something hard, a useful move is to ask: what’s the simplest version of this problem that still contains the thing I don’t understand? You might impose a symmetry or look at a limiting case. The point is to make it tractable without removing the essential difficulty.

Then you have to bring what you learned back to the original problem. Which features of the solution survive? Which were artifacts of the simplifying assumption? Can you relax that assumption a little and make progress?

That’s the behavior I’d like to see: a model that uses simpler problems to develop insight, checks that insight, and builds toward the harder question. Solving the warm-up is useful only if it teaches you something about the problem you actually care about.

r001.rationale: It mentions limiting cases and symmetry in general, but does not identify the flat-space limit or a black-hole problem.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says models should get better at choosing the warm-up problem themselves when tackling a hard research question.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like them to use warm-up problems more deliberately. In research, when you can’t solve the problem you care about, you look for a simpler problem that preserves some of the essential difficulty. Maybe there’s a symmetry you can impose, or a limit where you already know the answer. You solve that first to understand what your tools can do and where they fail.

The important part is then carrying that understanding back to the original problem. What made the simpler case solvable? Which assumptions were essential? What breaks when you remove them? I’d like a model to keep track of those questions, rather than solve a toy problem and treat that as evidence that the hard problem is solved.

And ideally, it would come up with the warm-up problems itself. Choosing a useful simpler question is a big part of doing research. Sometimes that choice is where the real insight happens.

r001.rationale: The response mentions using a known limit as a simpler warm-up, but does not identify the flat-space limit or connect it to a black-hole problem.
